Imagine you grew up in one culture — with its own language, food, clothing, celebrations, values, and ways of thinking. Now you move to a completely different country, or a new group of people with a very different culture moves into your community. Over time, through living side by side and interacting regularly, you begin to change. You pick up new habits. You start speaking a new language. You celebrate new holidays. Some of your old ways blend with the new ones. Some old ways fade away. Some you hold on to tightly.

This whole process — the cultural and psychological change that happens when two distinct cultures come into sustained, direct contact — is called acculturation.

It is both a process (something happening over time) and an outcome (the result of that process). The key word in understanding acculturation is contact — not brief, tourist-style contact, but deep, ongoing, unavoidable contact between two cultural groups.

Acculturation is not one single change. It is a broad shift across many areas of life:

  • Language — learning, adopting, or mixing a new language into daily life
  • Values and beliefs — what you consider right, wrong, important, or normal
  • Social behavior — how you greet people, show respect, interact in public
  • Food and dress — what you eat, how you dress, what feels "normal"
  • Religion and traditions — which rituals you practice, which you modify, which you abandon
  • Identity — how you see yourself, which group you feel you belong to

Acculturation touches the deepest parts of who a person is.

A critical thing to understand: acculturation is not a one-way street, even though people often think of it that way.

Yes, a minority group or an immigrant group is usually under greater pressure to change. But the dominant, or host, culture also absorbs things from the incoming group — food, music, words, fashion, ideas. Think of how much Mexican food has become part of everyday American life, or how much Indian vocabulary has entered British English. This cross-cultural borrowing happening on both sides is part of the full picture of acculturation.

Acculturation can be experienced at two levels:

At the group level: An entire cultural group undergoes acculturation — for example, when an indigenous tribe has sustained contact with a colonizing nation, or when a large immigrant community settles in a new country.

At the individual level: A single person undergoes acculturation — for example, an international student studying abroad, a refugee starting a new life in a foreign country, or someone who marries into a family from a very different cultural background.
The Four Ways a Person Can Respond to Acculturation

Not everyone responds to cultural contact the same way. Psychologists — most notably John W. Berry — have identified four main strategies people use, consciously or not:

1. Integration (also called Biculturalism)
The person embraces the new culture while also maintaining their original culture. They become genuinely comfortable in both worlds. This is often considered the healthiest and most balanced outcome. Example: An Indian immigrant who speaks fluent English at work, celebrates Diwali and Thanksgiving with equal enthusiasm, and feels at home in both cultures.

2. Assimilation
The person fully adopts the new culture and largely gives up their original one. They want to "blend in" completely. Example: A second-generation immigrant who speaks only the language of the new country, does not practice the customs of their parents' homeland, and identifies entirely with the new culture.

3. Separation
The person holds tightly to their original culture and rejects the new one. They live within their own community and minimize contact with the dominant culture. Example: A community that settles in a new country but keeps exclusively to itself, maintains its original language, customs, and social norms, and avoids mixing with the wider society.

4. Marginalization
The person loses connection with both their original culture and the new culture. They neither maintain their roots nor integrate into the new society. This is the most psychologically painful outcome. Example: Someone who, after years of being rejected by the dominant culture and having drifted away from their own heritage, feels they do not truly belong anywhere.
Acculturation vs. Words That Sound Similar

Since these words are often confused, here is a clear distinction:

Enculturation is the process of learning your own culture from birth — absorbing the values, norms, and behaviors of the society you grew up in. It happens naturally, through family, school, and community. It involves only one culture. Acculturation, on the other hand, involves two cultures coming into contact.

Assimilation is just one possible outcome of acculturation — the outcome in which a person fully adopts the new culture. Acculturation is the broader process; assimilation is one direction it can go.

Socialization is the general lifelong process of learning how to behave in society. Acculturation is more specific — it is about adapting when two different cultures meet.

Acculturation is not always smooth or comfortable. The psychological strain that comes from navigating two cultures — the confusion, the feeling of not fully belonging to either world, the pressure to change, the fear of losing your identity, or facing discrimination — is called acculturative stress (sometimes called culture shock in its more immediate form).

This stress is real and significant. Factors that affect how stressful acculturation is include: how different the two cultures are from each other, whether the person chose to move (like an immigrant seeking opportunity) or was forced to (like a refugee), whether the dominant society is welcoming or hostile, and how strong the person's original cultural identity is.
A Simple, Everyday Example to Tie It All Together

A young woman from Japan moves to Brazil for work. Over the next decade:

  • She learns Portuguese and begins to think in it naturally
  • She starts eating rice and beans daily but still makes miso soup at home
  • She celebrates Brazilian Carnival but still honors Japanese New Year traditions
  • Her sense of humor slowly shifts to match Brazilian social norms, but she still values the quiet discipline she was raised with
  • Her Brazilian colleagues start loving the Japanese snacks she brings to the office, and some even begin learning basic Japanese phrases

She has undergone acculturation. She has not become fully Brazilian (that would be assimilation), and she has not shut herself off from Brazil (that would be separation). She has integrated. She is both. And Brazil, in small but real ways, has been touched by her culture too.

If you ever need to state it plainly:

Acculturation is the process — and its result — of cultural and psychological change that occurs when individuals or groups from different cultures come into prolonged, direct contact with each other.

Everything else above is what that one sentence actually contains.
